summary: Specifies the requirements for an MPLS Transport Profile, a joint effort of ITU and IETF to support the needs of transport networks within the MPLS and PWE3 architectures.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5654 lists what the MPLS Transport Profile must support for packet transport networks. It sets requirements for paths, recovery, network layers, control and service quality rather than defining one protocol implementation.

questions: what are the requirements for mpls transport profile
how fast must mpls-tp recover from a failure
what does mpls-tp require for recovery
subtitle: Requirements for packet transport that combines MPLS with carrier transport-network operation.

tldr.problem: Carriers needed packet transport with reliability and operational behavior similar to established optical transport networks, while using MPLS where its features fit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists 115 requirements for the protocol building blocks of the MPLS Transport Profile. They cover path types, independent data and control planes, layering, recovery, rings and quality of service.
tldr.outcome: This is a joint IETF and ITU-T requirements document on the Standards Track, not a protocol definition. Other specifications provide the mechanisms that meet these requirements.

facts.label: Recovery target
facts.value: 50 ms from fault detection, spans under 1200 km

today: RFC 5654 is a Proposed Standard requirements specification. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs a Transport Profile
sections.content:
Packet services and applications increase demand on carrier networks. Existing optical transport technologies set expectations for reliability and operational simplicity, while carriers need packet transport that can meet service agreements and use network resources predictably.

Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS) already supports packet services, but not every MPLS feature fits transport-network operation and some transport capabilities are missing. MPLS-TP combines selected MPLS capabilities with transport-network practices. This RFC identifies protocol building blocks that must be available; it does not specify what each implementation must contain.
sections.plainLanguage: Carriers wanted to transport packets with the predictable operation of their transport networks. This document lists the capabilities that the MPLS toolkit must make available for that use.

sections.title: Transport Paths and Layer Networks
sections.content:
A transport network carries customer traffic between endpoints over paths that can remain in place for a long time. In MPLS-TP, a transport path corresponds to a Label Switched Path or a pseudowire. A layer network offers a transport service to a client layer and operates independently of the client using it.

The RFC distinguishes unidirectional paths, co-routed bidirectional paths that use the same route in both directions, and associated bidirectional paths made from two unidirectional paths that may take different routes. Transport-service traffic can be aggregated into transport paths, with operations and maintenance performed at each layer.
sections.plainLanguage: A transport path carries customer traffic through the network. Separate layers can carry and monitor that traffic without depending on the details of the client using the service.

sections.title: General and Layering Requirements
sections.content:
The MPLS-TP data plane must be a subset of the IETF MPLS data plane, and the design should reuse existing MPLS standards. It must interoperate with MPLS and PWE3 where appropriate, without requiring a gateway. It must support traffic-engineered point-to-point and point-to-multipoint paths, in the unidirectional and bidirectional forms listed in the RFC.

Both static provisioning through the management plane and dynamic provisioning through a control plane must be supported, and both may coexist. Static provisioning cannot depend on a control plane. Forwarding, OAM and protection must continue if the management or control plane fails. MPLS-TP must also support rings, including rings with at least 16 nodes.

MPLS-TP must carry client networks such as IP, MPLS, Ethernet and ATM, and its own paths must be transportable over server layers such as Ethernet, SONET/SDH and OTN. Its operation must be independent of those client and server layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements cover paths, provisioning and layer independence. The network must keep forwarding and recovery working even if its control or management connection fails.

sections.title: Data Plane and Control Plane
sections.content:
The data plane must be able to operate without IP forwarding and work only with MPLS labels. A path on a link must have a unique label, and its source must be identifiable at its destination. The data plane must preserve customer-traffic integrity as required by the service agreement and detect when integrity is lost.

A control plane is optional. If one is used, it must be independent of the data-plane topology and of any particular client or server control plane. It must set up the supported path types, configure OAM and recovery, and restart and relearn its state after failure without interrupting forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet-forwarding layer must keep working without IP forwarding or an active controller. A control plane can configure paths, but it must not be a single point of failure for traffic.

sections.title: Protection, Restoration and Recovery
sections.content:
MPLS-TP must provide protection and restoration at link, path, segment and end-to-end levels. Recovery paths must meet the service agreement. For networks with spans shorter than 1200 km, the requirements call for recovery within 50 ms from fault detection, and the operator must be able to require protection for all traffic on a protected path.

The profile must support 1+1 and 1:n protection, including shared protection resources where paths are not expected to need them at the same time. It must support both revertive and non-revertive operation, and switching must not create an uncontrolled traffic loop. Triggers can come from lower layers, OAM or management; a control plane should also be able to trigger restoration when present.

Operators must be able to configure protection paths, test recovery without triggering an actual switch, and determine the current protection status of paths.
sections.plainLanguage: When a path fails, the network must move traffic to protection or restoration resources within the service's recovery target. Operators must be able to test and monitor those mechanisms.

sections.title: Ring Networks and Quality of Service
sections.content:
Recovery must work in a single ring and in interconnected rings, and must protect traffic that crosses ring boundaries. In a 16-node ring with less than 1200 km of fiber, 1+1 and 1:1 protection switching must meet the 50 ms target from fault detection. The switching time must not depend on the number of LSPs crossing the ring. The default ring recovery behavior is bidirectional and revertive.

Quality-of-service mechanisms are required. They must support traffic classes, end-to-end bandwidth guarantees, services sensitive to delay and jitter, fair access to shared resources, guaranteed resources for in-band control and management, and flexible bandwidth allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: Ring networks have to protect traffic quickly, even when rings connect to one another. The profile also requires ways to reserve and manage bandwidth for services with different needs.

sections.title: Topics Specified Elsewhere
sections.content:
RFC 5654 does not define detailed requirements for network management, OAM or performance monitoring; it points to separate MPLS-TP requirements documents for those subjects. Security threats and defenses are covered by the security frameworks for MPLS/GMPLS and MPLS-TP.

The Security Considerations section itself refers readers to the security requirements discussion. The document's role is to identify the capabilities that the MPLS-TP protocol work must provide.
sections.plainLanguage: Network management, OAM, performance monitoring and security have separate requirements documents. This RFC points to those documents rather than repeating their rules.

items.title: Recovery time
items.text: 50 ms after fault detection for spans under 1200 km.

items.title: Protected traffic
items.text: Protection can be required for 100% of traffic on a path.

items.title: Ring size
items.text: Rings must support at least 16 nodes.
